primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Neural crest cells migrate extensively and form structures including melanocytes, peripheral sensory and autonomic ganglia, Schwann cells, adrenal medulla, and much of the craniofacial skeleton.
vignette: A fetus has a developmental disorder affecting melanocytes, dorsal root ganglia, and adrenal medullary cells.
lead: A defect in migration of which embryologic cell population best explains this combination?
distractor_notes: Paraxial mesoderm forms somites and axial musculoskeletal structures, not melanocytes or adrenal medulla.
Intermediate mesoderm forms much of the urogenital system.
Endoderm forms many epithelial linings and glandular organs.
Surface ectoderm forms epidermis and lens but not the listed peripheral neural and adrenal structures.
key_expl: Melanocytes, peripheral ganglia, Schwann cells, and adrenal medulla are classic neural crest derivatives.
objective: Recognize major neural crest derivatives from a multisystem developmental phenotype.
clues: peripheral ganglia and adrenal medulla involvement

sources.title: Neural Crest Disorders
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics provides background on developmental disorders caused by genetic disruption of cell development and migration.

sources.title: Embryonic Development
sources.support: NICHD describes early embryonic development and differentiation into tissues and organs.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Müllerian ducts normally form the uterus, fallopian tubes, cervix, and upper vagina; congenital agenesis causes absent uterine structures despite normal ovarian function and secondary sexual characteristics.
vignette: A 17-year-old girl has primary amenorrhea, normal breast development, normal pubic hair, and a 46,XX karyotype. Ultrasound shows normal ovaries but no uterus.
lead: Failure of development of which embryologic structure best explains these findings?
distractor_notes: Wolffian ducts form male internal reproductive structures under testosterone stimulation.
The urogenital sinus contributes to the lower vagina and urinary tract but does not form the uterus.
The genital tubercle contributes to external genital structures.
Mesonephric glomeruli are transient renal structures.
key_expl: In a 46,XX patient with normal ovaries and secondary sexual characteristics but absent uterus, Müllerian duct agenesis is the key defect.
objective: Identify Müllerian duct derivatives in a patient with congenital absence of the uterus.

sources.title: Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser syndrome
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics describes congenital absence or underdevelopment of the uterus and upper vagina in MRKH syndrome.

sources.title: Female Reproductive System
sources.support: NICHD describes the anatomy and development of female reproductive organs.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Defects in erythrocyte cytoskeletal proteins, often spectrin, impair horizontal membrane stability and produce elliptical red cells with variable hemolysis.
vignette: A 19-year-old man with mild chronic hemolysis has numerous elliptocytes on peripheral smear. Several family members have similar findings.
lead: Which cellular structure is most likely abnormal?
distractor_notes: Heme abnormalities cause hemoglobin synthesis disorders rather than inherited elliptocytosis.
Mature erythrocytes lack mitochondria.
Platelet dense-granule defects cause bleeding disorders.
Neutrophil granules are unrelated to red-cell shape.
key_expl: Hereditary elliptocytosis is caused by defects in red-cell membrane skeletal proteins that maintain cell shape and deformability.
objective: Relate hereditary elliptocytosis to erythrocyte membrane cytoskeletal instability.

sources.title: Hereditary elliptocytosis
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics describes inherited erythrocyte membrane protein defects causing elliptical red blood cells.

sources.title: SPTA1 gene
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics describes alpha-spectrin as an important structural component of the erythrocyte membrane cytoskeleton.

primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Severe beta-globin deficiency causes excess unpaired alpha chains, ineffective erythropoiesis, hemolysis, marrow expansion, and severe microcytic anemia beginning after fetal hemoglobin declines.
vignette: A 9-month-old infant has severe pallor, hepatosplenomegaly, growth failure, and marked microcytic anemia. Hemoglobin electrophoresis shows very little HbA and increased HbF.
distractor_notes: Iron deficiency does not typically cause severe infancy-onset anemia with marked HbF elevation and hepatosplenomegaly.
Alpha-thalassemia trait is usually mild and does not markedly increase HbF.
Sickle trait is generally asymptomatic and shows HbS on electrophoresis.
Hereditary spherocytosis causes normocytic hemolysis with spherocytes.
key_expl: Severe microcytic anemia beginning after the fetal-to-adult hemoglobin transition with little HbA and high HbF is classic beta-thalassemia major.
objective: Recognize beta-thalassemia major from infancy-onset severe microcytic anemia and electrophoresis findings.

sources.title: Beta thalassemia
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics describes severe beta-globin deficiency causing anemia, ineffective erythropoiesis, and increased fetal hemoglobin.

sources.title: HBB gene
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics describes HBB variants as causes of beta-thalassemia and other hemoglobin disorders.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Deficiency of the platelet GPIb-IX-V complex impairs platelet adhesion to von Willebrand factor at sites of vascular injury and causes thrombocytopenia with giant platelets.
vignette: A child has lifelong epistaxis and easy bruising. Platelet count is mildly reduced, giant platelets are present, and ristocetin-induced agglutination is abnormal and does not correct with normal plasma.
correct: GPIb receptor for von Willebrand factor
distractor_notes: GPIIb/IIIa deficiency causes Glanzmann thrombasthenia and impairs aggregation rather than vWF-mediated adhesion.
P2Y12 defects impair ADP-mediated activation but do not produce the classic giant-platelet Bernard-Soulier phenotype.
Thromboxane signaling is not the defining inherited defect here.
Tissue factor initiates coagulation but is not the platelet adhesion receptor in question.
key_expl: Bernard-Soulier syndrome is caused by loss of GPIb-IX-V, preventing platelet adhesion to vWF.
objective: Differentiate platelet adhesion defects from aggregation defects using receptor function.
clues: abnormal ristocetin response not corrected by plasma

sources.title: Bernard-Soulier syndrome
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics describes GPIb complex defects causing impaired platelet adhesion, thrombocytopenia, and giant platelets.

sources.title: GP1BA gene
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics describes GP1BA as encoding part of the platelet receptor for von Willebrand factor.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Deficiency of platelet GPIIb/IIIa prevents fibrinogen-mediated platelet cross-linking and aggregation while platelet adhesion remains intact.
vignette: A teenager has lifelong mucosal bleeding with normal platelet count. Ristocetin testing is normal, but platelet aggregation in response to ADP is absent.
lead: Which receptor is most likely deficient?
distractor_notes: GPIb deficiency causes Bernard-Soulier syndrome and abnormal ristocetin testing.
Factor VIII is a coagulation cofactor, not the platelet aggregation receptor.
tPA participates in fibrinolysis and does not mediate platelet cross-linking.
Protein C is an anticoagulant pathway protein.
key_expl: GPIIb/IIIa binds fibrinogen and links activated platelets; deficiency causes Glanzmann thrombasthenia.
objective: Identify the fibrinogen receptor defect in Glanzmann thrombasthenia.
clues: normal platelet count and ristocetin test

sources.title: Glanzmann thrombasthenia
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics describes GPIIb/IIIa deficiency causing impaired platelet aggregation and mucosal bleeding.

sources.title: ITGA2B gene
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics describes ITGA2B as encoding part of the platelet fibrinogen receptor.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Abnormal development of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches causes thymic hypoplasia and parathyroid hypoplasia, producing T-cell deficiency and hypocalcemia.
vignette: A newborn has a conotruncal cardiac defect, hypocalcemic tetany, and recurrent viral and fungal infections. Chest imaging shows absent thymic shadow.
lead: Which immune-cell population is most directly reduced?
distractor_notes: Neutrophil number is not the primary defect in thymic aplasia.
B cells may be present but antibody responses can be affected because T-cell help is deficient.
Eosinophils are not selectively depleted.
NK cells do not require thymic maturation and are not the defining deficient population.
key_expl: Thymic hypoplasia in DiGeorge syndrome impairs T-cell maturation.
objective: Connect thymic developmental failure with T-cell immunodeficiency.

sources.title: 22q11.2 deletion syndrome
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics describes thymic and parathyroid abnormalities causing immune deficiency and hypocalcemia.

sources.title: DiGeorge syndrome
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes DiGeorge syndrome as involving thymic hypoplasia and impaired T-cell development.

primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: WAS protein deficiency disrupts actin cytoskeleton signaling in hematopoietic cells, causing combined immunodeficiency, eczema, and microthrombocytopenia.
vignette: A 10-month-old boy has recurrent infections, eczema, and petechiae. Platelet count is low and platelets are unusually small.
distractor_notes: X-linked agammaglobulinemia causes absent B cells and small tonsils but not eczema with small platelets.
CGD causes phagocyte oxidative-burst failure without thrombocytopenia.
ITP causes isolated thrombocytopenia but not combined immunodeficiency and eczema.
Ataxia-telangiectasia causes ataxia and telangiectasias rather than microthrombocytopenia.
key_expl: The triad of eczema, recurrent infections, and thrombocytopenia with small platelets is classic Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome.
objective: Recognize Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome from its classic triad and platelet morphology.

sources.title: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics describes eczema, recurrent infections, and small-platelet thrombocytopenia in WAS.

sources.title: WAS gene
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics describes WAS protein as important for cytoskeletal signaling in blood cells.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: CD40 ligand deficiency on activated T cells prevents B-cell class-switch recombination, causing high or normal IgM with very low IgG, IgA, and IgE.
vignette: A 3-year-old boy has recurrent bacterial and opportunistic infections. Serum IgM is elevated, but IgG and IgA are markedly reduced.
lead: Which interaction is most likely defective?
correct: CD40 ligand on T cells binding CD40 on B cells
distractors: T-cell receptor binding MHC class I only
distractor_notes: B-cell antigen recognition can occur normally in hyper-IgM syndrome.
Terminal complement assembly is unrelated to immunoglobulin class switching.
GPIb-vWF mediates platelet adhesion.
TCR-MHC interactions are essential for T-cell activation but the classic molecular defect is CD40L-CD40 signaling.
key_expl: CD40L-CD40 signaling is required for immunoglobulin class-switch recombination; loss causes hyper-IgM syndrome.
objective: Explain hyper-IgM syndrome through defective T-cell help for B-cell class switching.

sources.title: X-linked hyper IgM syndrome
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics describes CD40LG variants causing failure of antibody class switching.

sources.title: CD40LG gene
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics describes CD40 ligand as essential for T-cell-dependent B-cell activation and class switching.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Selective failure of IgA production reduces mucosal antibody defense while other immunoglobulin classes are relatively preserved.
vignette: A 20-year-old woman has recurrent sinusitis and giardiasis. Serum IgA is nearly absent, while IgG and IgM are normal.
lead: Which immune function is most directly impaired?
distractor_notes: Oxidative burst failure causes CGD.
Thymic T-cell maturation defects occur in DiGeorge syndrome.
Terminal complement deficiency predisposes to Neisseria.
Platelet adhesion is unrelated to IgA.
key_expl: Secretory IgA is the principal immunoglobulin protecting many mucosal surfaces.
objective: Relate selective IgA deficiency to impaired mucosal immunity.

sources.title: Selective IgA deficiency
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics describes low IgA with recurrent respiratory and gastrointestinal infections.

sources.title: Immunoglobulins Blood Test
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes IgA as an antibody important in mucosal secretions.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Allergen cross-linking of IgE bound to FcεRI on mast cells triggers rapid release of histamine and other mediators.
vignette: Minutes after a bee sting, a patient develops urticaria, wheezing, and hypotension.
lead: Which immunologic event most directly initiates this reaction?
distractors: Immune complex deposition in small vessels
distractor_notes: Immune complex deposition causes type III hypersensitivity.
Cytotoxic T-cell reactions are type IV mechanisms.
Anti-basement-membrane IgG causes type II autoimmune injury.
Complement deficiency does not initiate anaphylaxis.
key_expl: Anaphylaxis is an IgE-mediated immediate hypersensitivity reaction triggered by mast-cell activation.
objective: Identify the initiating mechanism of type I hypersensitivity.

sources.title: Anaphylaxis
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes anaphylaxis as a rapid severe allergic reaction mediated by immune release of histamine and related mediators.

sources.title: Allergic Reactions
sources.support: NIAID describes IgE and mast-cell activation in immediate allergic reactions.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Circulating antigen-antibody immune complexes deposit in tissues, activate complement, and recruit inflammatory cells, causing fever, rash, arthralgia, and sometimes nephritis.
vignette: A patient develops fever, urticarial rash, arthralgia, and proteinuria 8 days after receiving a foreign-protein antiserum.
lead: Which hypersensitivity mechanism best explains the illness?
correct: Immune complex deposition with complement activation
distractor_notes: IgE-mediated disease occurs within minutes and produces anaphylaxis or immediate allergy.
Receptor-stimulating antibodies cause disorders such as Graves disease.
Direct T-cell killing is a type IV mechanism.
Loss of tolerance may underlie autoimmunity generally but does not specify the serum-sickness effector mechanism.
key_expl: Serum sickness is a classic type III hypersensitivity disorder caused by circulating immune complexes.
objective: Recognize type III hypersensitivity from delayed systemic immune-complex disease.

sources.title: Serum sickness
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes serum sickness as an immune-complex reaction after exposure to certain medicines or antiserum.

sources.title: Immune System and Disorders
sources.support: MedlinePlus provides background on antibody and immune-complex mediated inflammatory disorders.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Preformed recipient antibodies against donor ABO or HLA antigens activate complement and thrombosis immediately after reperfusion, causing rapid graft ischemia.
vignette: Minutes after a transplanted kidney is reperfused, it becomes cyanotic and produces no urine. Biopsy shows widespread thrombosis and fibrinoid necrosis.
lead: Which mechanism most likely caused this graft failure?
correct: Preexisting recipient antibodies against donor antigens
distractors: Newly generated donor-specific cytotoxic T cells over months
distractor_notes: T-cell clonal expansion cannot explain failure within minutes.
Chronic rejection develops over months to years.
Drug toxicity does not cause immediate diffuse graft thrombosis at reperfusion.
Infection does not cause this immediate vascular catastrophe.
key_expl: Hyperacute rejection occurs within minutes to hours from preformed recipient antibodies that trigger complement-mediated endothelial injury and thrombosis.
objective: Differentiate hyperacute rejection from acute and chronic rejection by timing and antibody mechanism.

sources.title: Transplant rejection
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes hyperacute rejection as occurring very quickly when preexisting antibodies attack the graft.

sources.title: Organ Transplantation
sources.support: NIAID describes immune responses against transplanted organs and the role of antibodies and cellular immunity.
